justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a fairly stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 756 is anchored closely to the most recent observed level, assuming continuity in whatever trend or mean-reversion dynamic was present at the time of the forecast. The slight upward drift to 758 at one week and 762 at one month reflects either a mild positive trend in the underlying series or a slight mean-reversion pull toward a longer-run average. The incremental increases are intentionally small because I lacked strong directional signals to justify a more aggressive slope, so the estimates essentially assume the status quo persists with only gradual change.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is the natural consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 36 units (738 to 774), reflecting relatively low overnight volatility and the assumption that short-run dynamics are fairly predictable. By one week, the interval widens to 66 units, and by one month it reaches 124 units, capturing the growing range of plausible paths the series could take. These widths were calibrated based on an implicit estimate of the series' historical volatility and the assumption that shocks are roughly independent across periods, meaning errors accumulate in something like a square-root-of-time fashion.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals. A sudden structural break — such as a major policy change, an external shock, or a regime shift in whatever market or system is being measured — could send the series well outside the one-month bounds. If the series is financial in nature, a sharp risk-off event or liquidity crisis could easily produce moves two to three times larger than the stated interval. On the upside, unexpectedly strong fundamental data or a catalyst specific to the underlying asset or indicator could push it through the upper bound of 824.

More broadly, my intervals assume relatively normal, continuous dynamics without fat-tailed jumps. If the true data-generating process has heavier tails than I assumed — which is common in financial and macroeconomic series — then the stated 90% intervals may actually be closer to 70–80% intervals in practice. The one-month horizon is where I have the least confidence in my calibration, as compounding uncertainty and the possibility of slow-moving but significant fundamental shifts make long-horizon forecasting inherently more treacherous than the mechanically widened interval might suggest.
